title: How to cut fabric for cross-stitch
subtitle: Calculating the size to cut and finishing the edges to prevent fraying
excerpt: Cutting cross-stitch fabric to the right size before starting prevents running short mid-project. The rule is to add at least 5 cm (2 inches) of fabric border on each side beyond the stitched design area. Aida frays badly when cut, so the raw edges need finishing immediately, either by hand overstitching, machine zigzag, or masking tape.
sourceNotes: Fabric preparation guidance from cross-stitch publisher guides and Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. It frays at cut edges and needs edge finishing before use.

content.text: before starting saves you from running out of fabric at the edge of the design. Add 5 cm (2 inches) of unstitched border all round the design area. This margin is used for mounting, hooping, and lacing. Cut generously rather than tight; unused border can always be trimmed, but short fabric cannot be extended.

Calculate the design area in inches or centimetres: (stitch count) divided by (fabric count) in each direction. A chart that is 70 stitches wide on 14-count Aida produces a design 5 inches (12.7 cm) wide. Add 4 inches (10 cm, being 2 inches each side) to get the cut size: 9 inches (22.7 cm) wide.

Cut Aida along the thread lines. Each square in the weave lines up with rows of threads. Cutting along a thread line gives a straight, even edge rather than a ragged diagonal. To find the thread line, mark the position with a pin, then use a blunt needle to draw a single thread out from the weave and cut along the visible groove.

Finish the cut edges immediately to prevent fraying. The three most practical methods: (1) fold each edge over twice and machine-sew a hem; (2) run a machine zigzag stitch along each edge; or (3) fold masking tape or washi tape over each raw edge. Tape is the quickest method and holds well for the duration of most projects.

Mark the centre of the cut piece with a pin or a length of basting thread in a colour that contrasts with the Aida. The centre mark should be visible but not permanent; a basting thread can be removed after the first few stitches of the design.

items.symptom: The cut edge is fraying badly before the project is finished
items.cause: Edge finishing was not done, or the tape came off partway through the project.
items.fix: Apply a fresh edge of masking tape, folding it over both sides of the raw edge. For a longer-term fix, hand-oversew the raw edge with a simple loop stitch in any spare thread.

items.symptom: The design runs too close to the edge of the fabric
items.cause: Insufficient border was left when cutting.
items.fix: For mounting or lacing, you need at least 3 cm of unstitched border all round. If the border is too narrow, the piece can still be framed in a hoop for display, which requires no border. For lacing onto card, add a strip of fabric to the back edge with fabric adhesive as a last resort.

content.text: With the fabric cut and the edges finished, find the centre of the piece and begin stitching from the centre outward. Working from the centre means the design stays balanced on the fabric rather than running off one edge.
